issues.legal_issue: Irreconcilable gifts in a will are governed by the later clause, so a later direction that property pass to others on the beneficiary’s death limits the beneficiary’s interest to a life interest.
material_facts: The will first described the daughter as owner of the remaining property, but later provided that the testator’s brothers would inherit that property on her death.
The daughter’s claim to ownership arose under the same will.
issues.conclusion: Read as a whole, the will conferred only a life interest on the daughter; the later clause prevailed over the inconsistent earlier description of her as owner.
issues.legal_principle: Section 88 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 provides that where two clauses of gifts in a will are irreconcilable, the last clause prevails because it represents the testator’s latest intention.

predicates.testamentary_property_dispute: The dispute concerns the interest created in property by a will.
predicates.will_clauses_conflict: The will contains clauses that cannot be reconciled as to the beneficiary’s interest in the same property.
predicates.later_clause_redirects_property_on_benef: A later clause directs that the property pass to others when the beneficiary dies.

issues.definition: When a property dispute concerns a will with conflicting clauses and the later clause redirects the property on the beneficiary’s death, the beneficiary receives only a life interest.

issues.legal_issue: A limited interest granted to a dependent widowed daughter in recognition of her pre-existing maintenance right against her father and his estate becomes full ownership under the rule enlarging a female Hindu’s limited interest, rather than remaining restricted under the exception for a grant without a pre-existing right.
material_facts: The daughter was widowed, destitute, dependent on her father, and maintained by him during his lifetime.
She had no property or other source of support, and the record did not show that she could obtain maintenance from her husband’s estate or other specified relatives.
The will gave her a life interest in part of the father’s property and reflected his concern for her maintenance after his death.
The father’s estate passed under the will to other beneficiaries, against whom her maintenance right could operate.
issues.conclusion: The daughter had a pre-existing right to maintenance against her father during his lifetime and against his estate after his death. The property given to her in lieu of that right became her full property under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956; Section 14(2) did not apply.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 19(1)(a), 21(vi), and 22(2) of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 support a widowed daughter’s maintenance rights against her father during his lifetime and against the estate taken by his heirs where she cannot maintain herself from the sources specified by the Act. Under Sections 14(1) and 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, a restricted grant in lieu of a pre-existing right is enlarged into full ownership; the exception applies to a grant made for the first time without such a right. V. Tulasamma v. V. Sesha Reddi and Badri Pershad v. Smt. Kanso Devi are relied on for that interpretation.

predicates.testamentary_property_dispute: The dispute concerns property given to a beneficiary under a will.
predicates.widowed_beneficiary_is_destitute: The beneficiary is a widowed daughter who is unable to maintain herself and depends on her father for support.
predicates.beneficiary_lacks_other_maintenance_sour: The beneficiary has no earnings or property and cannot obtain maintenance from the other sources relevant to her circumstances.
predicates.grant_recognizes_preexisting_maintenance: The property is given to the beneficiary in recognition of a maintenance right that existed before the will took effect.

issues.definition: When a will gives property to a destitute widowed beneficiary who lacks other maintenance sources in recognition of a pre-existing maintenance right, the restricted grant becomes full ownership.

issues.legal_issue: A daughter’s chance of inheriting from her father if he dies intestate is not a pre-existing legal right in his estate when he disposes of it by will.
material_facts: The daughter relied on her status as a class I heir to claim a pre-existing right to her father’s estate.
The father executed a will disposing of his property rather than dying intestate.
Her claim to succeed to the entire estate under the intestacy rules would have arisen only if he had died without a will.
issues.conclusion: The daughter had only a chance to succeed under intestacy, not a pre-existing legal right in the father’s estate; that chance alone could not support enlargement of her interest under Section 14(1).
issues.legal_principle: Section 8 and the Schedule to the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 govern succession to a male Hindu’s property when he dies intestate. A potential heir’s chance of succeeding if intestacy occurs is a spes successionis, not a pre-existing legal right in the owner’s estate.

predicates.succession_dispute: The dispute concerns whether a claimant had a pre-existing right in another person’s estate.
predicates.owner_disposed_of_property_by_will: The owner made a will disposing of the property before death.
predicates.claimant_would_inherit_only_if_owner_die: The claimant’s asserted entitlement to inherit would arise only if the owner died without a will.

issues.definition: When an owner disposes of property by will and the claimant would inherit only on intestacy, the claimant’s intestacy expectancy is not a pre-existing estate right.
